newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis mourn deaths, ponder cause of air crash.
newsitem.headline: Israelis mourn deaths, ponder cause of air crash.

text.p: Not since Israelis lost their prime minister to an assassin's bullet has the outpouring of grief been so intense.

The death of 73 soldiers in a helicopter collision on Tuesday has plunged the Jewish state into successive days of mourning with the names of victims being announced in hourly radio bulletins and funerals being broadcast on television.
Shops and restaurants were shut on Wednesday with signs in windows saying: "Closed in light of the national tragedy".
Grim-faced leaders could not explain what caused the worst crash in the country's military history but said the soldiers died on a mission to protect Israel.

"The people here know better than any how these soldiers and heroic commanders take risks to protect the residents of the north," said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on a visit to the site of the crash near the Lebanese border.
The helicopters were flying to a 15 km (nine mile)-wide occupation zone in south Lebanon that the Jewish state carved out in 1985 to prevent guerrilla attacks on northern Israel.
"Our quest for peace involves constant sacrifices, constant risks," he told reporters.
As rescue workers identified the bodies, army authorities released the names of more and more soldiers until it seemed nearly every Israeli could trace a connection to at least one of the victims.
"Everyone knows at least one person who's on his way to a funeral today," said Noa Shimoni, a university student whose friend from high school was among the dead.
"This is like the Rabin assassination all over again," she said, referring to the huge outpouring of grief after a right wing assassin murdered Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin on November 3, 1995.
In Beirut, the pro-Iranian Hizbollah group fighting to expel Israel from Lebanon said the crash was an act of God.

"We consider what happened a success granted by God...I will use this occasion to express big happiness and ask our people and loved ones to pray to God and thank him," said Hizbollah deputy chief Sheikh Na'eem Qassem.
Israel's army chief Amnon Shahak said in a statement to soldiers that Israeli troops would remain in Lebanon.
"The army is engaged in a never-ending war, a drawn-out war to defend the state of Israel on its northern borders and throughout the country," he said.
"The mission grows more and more difficult and sometimes hits too close to home...(but) we will strengthen ourselves and comfort ourselves with the belief that the army can overcome this tragedy."
An official period of national mourning declared by the government was to continue until Thursday night.

Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai named a five-man committee to investigate the disaster but officials refused to speculate on its cause. Witnesses reported explosions after the helicopters crashed, apparently from ammunition in the cargo.

Israelis, including politicians across the spectrum, mourned the loss of life. Most of the dead were around the age of 20. In Israel's previous worst military air disaster, 54 paratroopers died in a helicopter crash in 1977.
